notes.meaning: David organized the gatekeepers from the tribe of Levi into regular shifts. Their job was to guard the sanctuary doors and ensure only clean and authorized people entered. Meshelemiah came from the Korahite family line, descended from an ancestor named Asaph (or Ebiasaph), rather than the well-known temple singer.

Meshelemiah was blessed with seven sons, starting with his firstborn, Zechariah. These sons were appointed as leaders over distinct groups of gatekeepers. Their families formed trusted units responsible for guarding the house of God.

Obed-edom had eight sons, listed here in order from the oldest to the youngest. God blessed his family with many children because he had reverently sheltered the ark of the covenant in his home. His large family provided many dependable men to serve the Lord.

Shemaiah, Obed-edom's firstborn son, had capable sons and brothers who became leaders in their clan. These men needed physical strength and great courage because their guard duties included opening heavy gates and stopping disorders or intruders. They stood as a dependable military guard over the sacred courts.

A total of sixty-two gatekeepers came from the family of Obed-edom. Every one of these sons, grandsons, and relatives was strong and well suited for the demanding work at the gates. God's earlier blessing on this family bore lasting fruit in their humble service.

Meshelemiah's immediate family contributed eighteen capable men to the guard force. Together with his sons, these kinsmen had the strength and resolve needed to stand watch. Alongside Obed-edom's family, they formed the main group of Korahite gatekeepers.

Hosah represented the Merarite branch of Levites and had thirteen sons and relatives in this ministry. Hosah chose his son Shimri to lead the group even though Shimri was not the firstborn, likely because the older brother had died or Shimri was best suited for leadership. These Merarite guards served faithfully alongside their Korahite brothers.

These leaders and their families were organized into regular rotations to serve at the house of the Lord. Just like the priests and musicians, the gatekeepers took turns on duty week by week. In God's eyes, guarding His dwelling was holy and honorable work, just like offering sacrifices or singing praise.

The gatekeepers cast lots to decide which family would guard which gate. Casting lots was an ancient way of letting God make the final choice without showing human favoritism. Older and younger families, large and small, were treated equally before the Lord.

The lot for the East Gate went to Shelemiah (also called Meshelemiah), placing his family at the main entrance. His firstborn son Zechariah was chosen for the North Gate and was known as a wise counselor. Guarding the sanctuary required sound judgment and wisdom just as much as physical strength.

The South Gate was assigned by lot to Obed-edom, and his sons were given charge of the nearby storehouses. These storehouses held grain, wine, and other offerings brought for the upkeep of the temple and the priests. Obed-edom's family was trusted to watch over both the gate and the sacred supplies.

The West Gate and the Shallecheth Gate along the ascending highway were assigned to Hosah. The Shallecheth Gate was likely the gate where refuse and ashes from the temple courts were carried out. Guards were posted at matched positions to ensure all sides remained secure day and night.

Every day twenty-four gatekeepers stood guard around the sanctuary. Six were placed at the busy east entrance, four at the north, four at the south, four at the storehouse, and six along the western court and highway. This clear schedule kept the holy courts guarded from every direction.

This statement concludes the list of gatekeeper divisions assigned to the temple. All of these men belonged either to the Korahites or the Merarites within the tribe of Levi. God provided orderly leadership for every entrance to His house.

Other Levites were appointed to guard the sacred treasuries. One treasury held the everyday tithes, holy vessels, and supplies needed to run the temple, while another held treasures dedicated to God. These stewards carried the solemn trust of protecting the church's wealth for God's glory.

The family of Ladan, belonging to the Gershonite clan of Levites, looked after the general treasuries of the temple. Zetham and his brother Joel, descendants of Jehieli, served as the chief officers in charge. They managed the grain, wine, sacred vessels, and regular tithes needed for worship.

Levites from the four main branches of Kohath were given financial responsibilities. Shebuel, a descendant of Moses through Gershom, served as the chief officer over all the treasuries. This placed the family of Moses right at the heart of managing the Lord's house.

Shebuel's relatives through Moses' other son, Eliezer, are traced down through Rehabiah to Shelomith. These family records showed the exact line of descent for those holding high office. God honored the family of Moses by calling them to sacred leadership.

Shelomith and his relatives had charge of the treasures dedicated to God by King David, army commanders, and clan leaders. It was customary to set aside a portion of plunder taken in war as an offering of gratitude to the Lord. These dedicated goods were kept in reserve to build, repair, and maintain the house of God.

Shelomith also guarded gifts that had been dedicated long before David, including spoils given by Samuel, King Saul, Abner, and Joab. Over many decades, Israel's leaders had honored God by donating the spoils of victory to His sanctuary. All these historic treasures were kept safe under Shelomith's trustworthy care.

Chenaniah and his sons, from the Izharite family, were appointed to duties outside the temple grounds. They served across the land as officers and judges to settle disputes and teach God's law. Because God's law was the foundation of the nation, Levites made ideal civic leaders and teachers of justice.

Hashabiah and seventeen hundred capable men from the Hebronite clan were placed over the region west of the Jordan River. They managed both the work of the Lord and the service of the king, helping with temple offerings and civil administration. In Israel, serving God and keeping public order went hand in hand.

Near the end of David's forty-year reign, official records were examined to find qualified leaders among the Hebronites living at Jazer in Gilead. David appointed Jerijah and twenty-seven hundred clan leaders over the tribes east of the Jordan River—Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh. Because these eastern tribes lived far from the capital on the border, they needed a large group of wise leaders to keep them faithful to God and loyal to the king.
